newsitem.title: FRANCE: MOTOR RACING-ALBORETO DRIVES PORSCHE PROTOTYPE TO VICTORY.
newsitem.headline: MOTOR RACING-ALBORETO DRIVES PORSCHE PROTOTYPE TO VICTORY.

text.p: Italian Michele Alboreto realised a dream when he drove the Joest TWR Porsche prototype to the German team's second successive Le Mans 24 Hours victory on Sunday.

"I've had this dream for a long time of winning this race and now it's come true," Alboreto, 40, said after partnering another ex-Formula One driver, Stefan Johansson of Sweden, and Dane Tom Kristensen in the winning car.

It was a record 15th Le Mans win for Porsche and a fourth for the Reinhold Joest team, whose prototype designed by Briton Tom Walkinshaw followed victories in 1984, 1985 and last year, all with the number 7.
"We did a good job. We're going to try to repeat this victory next year," said Alboreto, who won five of his 194 grands prix and who was Formula One world championship runner-up with Ferrari in 1985.

"We had to put maximum pressure on the factory cars," Alboreto said after co-driver Kristensen set the record for the 13.6-km track, lapping in three minutes 45.068 seconds at an average speed of 217.534 kph.
McLaren BMW F1GTRs occupied second and third place after the two factory Porsche 911 GT1s who shared the lead for two-thirds of the race both failed to finish.

The second-placed car was driven by Frenchmen Jean-Marc Gounon and Pierre-Henri Raphanel and Anders Olofsson of Sweden, the other by Dutchman Peter Kox, Roberto Ravaglia of Italy and France's Eric Helary.

The works Porsche driven by Frenchman Bob Wollek, Hans Stuck of Germany and Belgium's Thierry Boutsen crashed out early on Sunday morning, spinning off with Wollek at the wheel on the Arnage bend. Wollek was unhurt.
Two hours from the finish, the other Porsche driven by German Ralf Kelleners caught fire when it was in the lead.
Kelleners, who shared the driving with Frenchmen Yannick Dalmas, three times winner at Le Mans, and Emmanuel Collard, escaped from the blazing car unhurt.
Dalmas, speaking shortly before the accident, said: "I get the feeling less of taking part in an endurance race than a sprint. There hasn't been a let- up since the start."

A McLaren driven by Briton Andrew Scott -- with compatriot Ray Bellm and Masanori Sekiya of Japan -- also burst into flames some 20 minutes later when it was in fifth place at the same spot after the Mulsanne rise. Scott also escaped unhurt.
Two cars caught fire on Saturday evening and only 17 cars, eight less than last year, completed the race from an entry of 48.
The Chrysler Viper of Japan's Soheil Ayari and Briton Perry McCarthy's Pangoz GTR both caught fire as they spun off course early in the race. The drivers were unhurt.
French veteran Henri Pescarolo, in a record 31st Le Mans, was seventh in his Courage C36.
Of the three Nissan R390s that started the race with hight hopes, only one finished, in 12th place.
